planting.note: Set out rhizome divisions or potted pups after all frost danger has passed into rich, moisture-retentive soil; this Himalayan foothill species is one of the more cold-tolerant ornamental bananas and can be grown as a die-back perennial into zone 7 with heavy mulching.

directions: Give this vigorous species deep, humus-rich soil and steady moisture, since its broad paddle leaves wilt quickly in dry spells. The trunks and leaf undersides often show attractive maroon-red mottling, most pronounced on selections like 'Red Tiger'. Where winters exceed the plant's tolerance, cut the pseudostem back after hard frost and mulch heavily over the rhizome to protect it for spring resprouting. Feed monthly through the growing season with a balanced fertilizer to sustain the huge leaf canopy.

planting.note: Plant offsets or seedlings after nights stay reliably warm; this compact species is grown chiefly for its upright, waxy scarlet-and-yellow bracts rather than for fruit.

directions: Site in bright, filtered light with shelter from strong wind, which can shred the relatively small leaves. Keep the root zone consistently moist but not waterlogged, and mulch to buffer soil temperature swings. The brilliant red flower spike stands upright above the foliage for weeks, making this one of the showiest small ornamental bananas for a container or protected courtyard planting. In marginal zones, overwinter potted specimens indoors in bright light since the species has little cold tolerance.

planting.note: Plant divisions in warm soil after frost danger passes; grown as a flowering ornamental rather than for edible fruit, valued for its brick-orange inflorescence held well above the foliage.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist soil under high dappled shade to filtered sun, replicating the understory conditions of its native Southeast Asian hill forests. This compact species flowers reliably even as a young plant, sending up a distinctive burnt-orange to brick-red bract cluster that persists for several weeks. It has minimal frost tolerance, so gardeners outside zone 9 should treat it as a container specimen brought indoors before the first cold snap. Divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Set out young plants after frost danger passes in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; unlike Ensete ventricosum this species suckers less freely and, like most Ensete, dies after flowering once mature.

directions: Provide a large, sheltered planting area with rich soil and consistent irrigation, as the massive glaucous-blue trunk and huge waxy leaves demand heavy feeding to reach full size. This species is monocarpic, meaning each pseudostem flowers once and then dies, so plan for its dramatic but finite lifespan rather than a permanent clump like suckering bananas. The powdery blue-white bloom on the trunk and leaf undersides is its signature ornamental feature, most vivid in strong indirect light. In cooler zones grow in a large container that can be moved under cover well before frost, since it has essentially no cold hardiness once established outdoors.
